headline: Singapore Pays Citizens to Read—and the Habit Might Stick
meta_description: Singapore launched a government program rewarding citizens with cash for reading time, banking on behavioral science to boost a fading habit.
summary_short: Singapore is paying people to read books, offering cash rewards for time spent with literature. Experts say the incentive could make reading a lasting habit.
body:
Singapore has launched an unusual experiment in habit formation: a government program that pays citizens cash for time spent reading. The rewards are modest—it takes fifty daily 15-minute reading sessions to earn just one Singapore dollar, equivalent to about $0.78 U.S.—yet behavioral scientists believe the program could work anyway. Ivo Vlaev, a professor of behavioral psychology at the National University of Singapore, explains that "incentives do not always work in proportion to their monetary value." What matters is that people enjoy working toward concrete goals and accumulating points, even when the monetary payoff is small.

The initiative reflects a growing concern that reading is becoming a lost habit. Rather than accept this decline, Singapore's government decided to test whether financial motivation could reverse the trend. The psychology here is subtle: people respond to the structure of achievement itself, not just the dollars earned. By making reading quantifiable and rewarding, the program creates a framework for building a new routine.

Singapore joins other regions finding creative ways to meet people where they actually are. In Assam, India, post offices have begun offering eye screenings—a simple strategy since residents visit post offices regularly but might never travel to a clinic. In that pilot program, 82 percent of people who were tested and needed glasses said they were wearing spectacles for the first time. With India operating nearly 165,000 post offices, using them as health screening facilities could reach millions who currently lack access to basic vision care. These efforts share a common logic: remove barriers, make essential services convenient, and change follows.
quick_facts: Singapore government pays citizens cash rewards for time reading
Fifty 15-minute reading sessions earn one Singapore dollar ($0.78 USD)
Behavioral science shows incentives work beyond their monetary value
Assam post offices screen vision; 82% of those needing glasses got them for first time
India has nearly 165,000 post offices that could expand health services
